payload.headline: Tesla stalls just under resistance at 380.15 while margins and cash flow keep shrinking

summary.thesis: Tesla is a strong-balance-sheet company whose sales have stalled and whose margins and cash flow are falling, yet the price of 380.11 sits near the top of its own price-to-sales history and far above every cash-flow value.
summary.decision: Long-term: avoid. Swing: no trade while the price is stuck in a flat range before the 2027-01-27 report.
summary.act_at: Reconsider near 293.94 if margins stop falling; no swing trade unless there is a close above 396.23 or below 364.02

payload.happening: The stock closed at 380.11, up 0.1%. That leaves it just under a heavily tested ceiling at 380.15–388.56, which the price has touched 9 times. There is no news since the last note. The next earnings report is due 2027-01-27, and options price a 15.4% move by the 2027-01-15 expiry, which comes before that report.
payload.business: The figures that change the business all point the wrong way. Sales growth in the latest quarter was -0.17% compared with a year earlier, down from 15.78% two quarters ago. Operating margin (the profit kept from each dollar of sales before interest and tax) fell to 3.35% from 4.74%. Free cash flow over the past twelve months dropped to 3.3B from 6.8B. Filings flag inventory up 15% while sales were up 0%, and unsold cars can force price cuts that squeeze margins further. They also flag that each dollar invested now earns 5¢ a year, against 33¢ three years ago. What is not at risk is survival: Tesla holds 37.5B of net cash and 45.4B of total liquidity against 8.0B of debt. R&D at 8.56% of revenue and dilution of only 0.43% a year are not the problem either. The committee's macro view of a tech market in a downtrend with elevated fear affects sentiment, not the business itself.

worth.text: There are two ways to value Tesla here, and they disagree sharply. A discounted cash flow (DCF) model, which values the company on the cash it is expected to produce, gives 19.94 in the bear case, 24.52 in the base case and 43.93 in the bull case. Even if growth started at 30% a year, the DCF value would only reach 44.01. The other method assumes the market keeps paying what it has paid before for each dollar of Tesla's sales. On that basis the range is 203.8 to 399.81, with 293.94 in the middle. At 380.11 the stock trades at 14.5 times sales and 418.3 times trailing earnings. That price-to-sales level sits at the 72nd percentile of Tesla's own past five years. Filings estimate that the price needs about 52% growth a year, while the company has delivered 3% a year over three years. The whole gap between the methods comes down to one assumption: does the market keep valuing Tesla on a sales multiple, or start valuing it on today's cash flow? I use the own-history range as the fair-value band. The price is already near its top.
worth.key_assumption: The market keeps valuing Tesla within its own 5-year price-to-sales range instead of on current free cash flow.

bull: Tesla has 37.5B of net cash and 45.4B of liquidity, so it can fund heavy spending through a weak stretch.
Analysts' next-year earnings growth of 25% is one of the valuation inputs. If that growth shows up, the DCF bull value is 43.93 and the price-to-sales ceiling is 399.81.
Options traders are leaning toward calls: the put/call open-interest ratio is 0.82, and the busiest call strike is 400 with 25777 contracts open.
bear: Free cash flow halved to 3.3B from 6.8B, and operating margin fell to 3.35% from 4.74%.
Inventory rose 15% while quarterly sales were flat at -0.17%, which raises the risk of price cuts.
Every DCF value sits at or below 43.93, against a price of 380.11. That price needs about 52% growth a year, versus 3% a year delivered over three years.

levels.what: Today's close. It is near the top of the own-history range and many times the DCF base value of 24.52.
The top of the own-history price-to-sales range. Above it, even the generous method calls the stock expensive.
The middle of the own-history range. At this level the stock no longer needs a top-of-range multiple, so it earns a fresh look if operating margin stops falling below 3.35%.

longterm.why: Sales have stalled, and margins and cash flow are shrinking, yet the price still assumes a top-of-history multiple. The business is graded D and the rules committee call is Reduce.

swing.why: The trend is a flat range. The 20-, 50- and 200-day averages (386.26, 375.49 and 382.27) are all flat. Support at 364.02–368.6 and resistance at 380.15–388.56 are both close compared with the 16.0 average daily move, so a stop would sit inside normal noise. A close above 396.23 or below 364.02 would show a direction.

decision.timing: No new position before the 2027-01-27 report, which is the next real test of margins and cash flow; options price a 5.2% move by 2026-11-20 and 15.4% by 2027-01-15, so range swings in between are noise, not signal.

change_mind: If the 2027-01-27 report shows operating margin back above 4.74% and quarterly sales growth back toward 15.78%, the long-term view would turn from avoid to wait.
If the price falls to 293.94 (the middle of the own-history range) and operating margin holds at 3.35% or better, the long-term view would turn to buy.
A daily close above 396.23 (the top of the upper resistance zone) or below 364.02 (the bottom of nearer support) would end the range and justify a swing setup in that direction.
payload.what_changed: Unchanged: still avoid and no trade; the price is stuck just under resistance at 380.15, there is no news since the last note, and the falling margins and cash flow behind yesterday's call have not changed.
payload.label: Research, not advice.
